text:
IN THE SUPREME COURT OF BRITISH COLUMBIA

Citation:

Ross v. Hammer,

2023 BCSC 2306

Date: 20231128

Docket:
M240446

Registry: New Westminster

Between:

Leanne
Ross

Plaintiff

And:

Michael
James Hammer and

Kathleen Ai Wong

Defendants

Before: Master Krentz

Oral Reasons for Judgment

In Chambers

Counsel for the Plaintiff:

M.A.
McDonald

Counsel for the Defendants:

A.
Laudadio

Place and Date of Hearing:

New
Westminster, B.C.

November
16, 2023

Place and Date of Judgment:

New
Westminster, B.C.

November
28, 2023

[
1
]

THE COURT:
The
following is my decision in this matter. There are cross‑applications
before me and pursuant to the defendants' application filed on October 25,
2023, they seek an order that the plaintiff's action be stayed until the Civil
Resolution Tribunal (“CRT”) determines whether the plaintiff's injuries arising
from a motor vehicle accident in September 2020 are minor injuries within

s. 133
of the
Civil Resolution Tribunal Act
, S.B.C. 2012, c. 25

[
CRTA
].

[
2
]

The plaintiff filed an application on October 31,
2023, seeking to strike that portion of the response to the civil claim that may
raise as a defence that the injuries are minor injuries.

[
3
]

The relevant provisions of the
CRTA
came
into force on April 1, 2019. Effective that date, in respect of a motor-vehicle
accident, the Legislature gave the CRT jurisdiction to determine whether an
injury alleged in respect of an accident is a minor injury for the purposes of
the
Insurance (Vehicle) Act
,

R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 231. That
jurisdiction is no longer effective as of May 1, 2021, when the Province
moved into a full no‑fault system.

[
4
]

Regarding the CRT's jurisdiction,
s. 133(1)
(b)
of the
CRTA

provides as follows:

… [T]he tribunal has jurisdiction in a
dispute, in respect of an accident, over a claim concerning one or more of the
following:

…

(b)        the determination of whether an
injury is a minor injury for the purposes of the
Insurance (Vehicle) Act
.

[
5
]

The CRT's jurisdiction under
s. 133(1)
(b)
is exclusive and it is final and binding on the parties, subject only to
judicial review in accordance with the provisions of the
CRTA
.

[
6
]

A minor injury is one that does not result in
serious impairment or a permanent serious disfigurement and is a pain‑related
syndrome, a psychiatric condition, a laceration, strain, whiplash‑associated
injury, a temporomandibular joint disorder (“TMJ”) disorder or a concussion
that does not result in incapacity. A serious impairment is described as an
impairment that has not resolved within 12 months and meets the prescribed
criteria.

[
7
]

Under the Regulations, those prescribed criteria
are described as the plaintiff's substantial inability to perform the essential
tasks of daily living or their regular employment despite reasonable efforts at
accommodation.

[
8
]

Contemporaneously with the Regulations coming
into force, the Trial Lawyers Association of British Columbia challenged the
constitutional validity of the amendments in that they are an impermissible
derogation from the exclusive superior court jurisdiction and denies motor
vehicle accident victims their constitutional rights of access to the courts.

[
9
]

In upholding that challenge, Chief Justice
Hinkson in
Trial Lawyers Association of British Columbia v. British Columbia
(Attorney General)
,
2021 BCSC 348
, at para.
361
noted that the
Attorney General's claim that the CRT process will be faster is speculation at
best, as the CRT has no record of handling the volume of cases anticipated by
the Attorney General.

[
10
]

Therefore, Chief Justice Hinkson found the judicial powers conferred
under the CRT pursuant to
s. 133
were not necessarily incidental to the Legislature's
policy goals of enhancing access to justice. The Chief Justice further found
that the judicial powers were neither subsidiary nor ancillary to any general
administrative functions.

[
11
]

The Chief Justice concluded that
s. 133(1)
(b) and (c) violated

s. 96
of the
Constitution Act
,
1867
, so he declared those
sections and portions of
s. 16.1
of the
CRTA
to be of no force or
effect. The Attorney General appealed the decision and in May 2022, the appeal
was allowed (
British Columbia (Attorney General) v. Trial Lawyers
Association of British Columbia
,
2022 BCCA 163
), as the Court of Appeal
found that the amendments do not impermissibly invade the core jurisdiction of
the Supreme Court of British Columbia for the following reasons.

[
12
]

The Court of Appeal found that there were several avenues for the
Supreme Court to retain jurisdiction over the sort of motor vehicle claims at
issue in the litigation. They found the Supreme Court plays a robust role on
judicial reviews and the scheme was enacted to further an important societal
objective.

[
13
]

The Province had identified that the existing system of compensating
for minor personal injuries in tort was threatening the validity of the public
insurer, the Insurance Corporation of British Columbia (“ICBC”) and equally the
actual compensation recovered by the victims of these minor injuries.

[
14
]

They found the impugned scheme to be an experiment in a new form of
access to justice and represents an integrated comprehensive effort at reform
directed at a social mischief identified by other branches of government.

[
15
]

In July 2022, Justice Funt in
Madden v.
Ampabeng,
(28 July 2022), Vancouver File M1912977 (B.C.S.C.) confirmed that
pursuant to
s. 16.1(2)
(a) of the
CRTA
that he was required to stay
an action that was set for trial to commence the next month, pending the minor
injury determination by the CRT.

[
16
]

Later in
Carter v. Uytterhagen
(24 Feb 2023), Vancouver File
M202798 (B.C.S.C.), Justice Branch in a similar application found he had no other
option but to grant the order as the cited section simply does not allow for
considerations of fairness or timeliness to enter into the decision of whether
or not the mandatory order should issue. He found support in the
Madden
decision,
wherein Funt J. issued a stay without finding it necessary to consider fairness
or timeliness issues generally or any other factors specifically.

[
17
]

Justice Branch concluded the only aspect over
which he had discretion related to the question of costs. He said as much as he
sympathized with the plaintiff's concerns, he found it was too early for the
court to make a determination as to costs. Specifically, he noted at para. 4,
consideration of proper cost orders would require more sensitive consideration
of:

…. (1) the
merits of the plaintiff's position, both generally and in relation to whether
or not the injuries alleged are minor; and (2) a consideration of precisely
when any costs or disbursements were incurred … .

[
18
]

In conclusion, he found the appropriate order is to stay the action
and adjourn the trial, but also confirmed that costs of the application and the
action more generally could be brought forward for determination after the CRT
had made its determination on whether or not this is a minor injury.

[
19
]

In this action on March 8, 2023, the defendants'
counsel wrote to plaintiff's counsel as follows:

As you are
likely aware, on December 22, 2022, the Supreme Court of Canada dismissed the
application for leave to appeal the judgment of the
Trial Lawyers
Association of British Columbia v. British Columbia (Attorney General)
,

2022
BCCA 163
. As a result, the [CRT] has exclusive jurisdiction to determine
whether an injury is a
minor injury
and has specialized expertise to
determine liability and damages for personal injury of up to $50,000. …

Defendants’ counsel then indicated that:

… The Defendants'
position is that your client's alleged injuries fall within the definition of
"
minor injury
" as set out in the [regulations]. …

[
20
]

They followed up on the inquiry with another letter dated August 3,
2023, again asking that the plaintiff to stay the action and adjourn the trial
pending a determination by the CRT, if not, they would bring forward an
application for a stay.

[
21
]

In response to the application for a stay, the plaintiff submits
that the response to the civil claim fails to plead the jurisdiction of the CRT
or even cite as an authority the
CRTA
. The plaintiff submits there is no
reference to the adjudication of minor injury by the CRT in the
Insurance
(Vehicle) Act
, which is the legislation primarily pled by the defendants.

[
22
]

The plaintiff further notes that as recently as November 7, in‑house
ICBC counsel confirmed they were not amending their response to the civil
claim.

[
23
]

Before I analyze the stay application, I will deal with the
plaintiff's application to strike pleadings and I do so because if that
application is successful, then the defendants' application is rendered moot. I
also do so on the assumption that the minor injury issue was properly pled.

[
24
]

In her submission the plaintiff acknowledged the following. An
application to strike pleadings, particularly in personal injury law, is quite
extraordinary. If the defence correctly pleads minor injury, the two Supreme
Court decisions that I just referred to, state that the court has no choice but
to stay the action and refer it to the CRT. Also, the court is not to consider
the interests of justice and fairness or weigh evidence.

[
25
]

The plaintiff properly raises the question, what is the plaintiff to
do when their case clearly does not fall within the definition of "minor
injury"? They note that referring the matter to the CRT results in the
action being sidelined for about 18 months. At the end of that 18 months, if
the CRT determines it is not a minor injury and if no trial date is
outstanding, a plaintiff faces another 18 to 24 months to wait for a Supreme
Court trial.

[
26
]

The plaintiff submits that she amended her notice of civil claim on
October 23, 2023 to allege only injuries that are not covered by the minor
injury regulation. Notwithstanding these amendments, the defence is determined
to proceed with the stay application.

[
27
]

In amending the notice of civil claim, she narrowed her claim to
seek compensation for the following serious injuries: bilateral adhesive
capsulitis (also known as frozen shoulders); neurological injury to her right
C6-7 nerve root; and a pain syndrome resulting in serious impairment.

[
28
]

The plaintiff alleges that most of her post‑accident care was
through a clinic which offers treatment from various practitioners. She has had
over 250 treatment sessions from October 6, 2020 to September 24, 2023, and
continues to attend weekly therapy.

[
29
]

The plaintiff submits that prior to the accident, she had no
symptoms in any of the traumatized areas, as noted on the intake diagram from a
clinic. She says she was in constant pain for the first year following the
accident. Both her shoulders were "frozen," which was sore and
painful. Her right C6‑7 neurological pain made her right arm "quite
useless."

[
30
]

The plaintiff says a physiatrist commenced a series of cortisone
injections to thaw the shoulders. She says currently she still has bilateral
shoulder and cervical nerve root pain daily. It is worse at the end of the day
and aggravated by typing at a computer or even lying down.

[
31
]

Vocationally, she says she was disabled from working any job for
approximately one year. Just prior to the accident, she had been working for a
jewellery store. She was responsible for setting up and breaking down displays,
shipping, receiving, inventory and customer service.

[
32
]

In 2021, she accepted a job in student services at the Justice Institute
in New Westminster. Her job is sedentary and allows her to take frequent breaks.
She finds it painful to use a computer and the mouse. She uses a heating pad
daily to loosen her shoulders in the area near her cervical nerve root injury
within an hour of commencing work. She could never return to working in the job
she had before.

[
33
]

The plaintiff is married and she has three children. Prior to the
accident, she did most of the housework, including: laundry, cleaning and meal
preparation. After the accident, she cannot do anything that requires bending forward,
lifting and reaching. All of her family activities have been restricted. In
addition, the plaintiff was examined by a physiatrist and in his recent report,
he opines that the injuries do not fall within the minor injury regulations.

[
34
]

The plaintiff is also seeing a counsellor to
deal with emotional issues. The counsellor has reported the following:

The plaintiff
describes her emotional impact of the accident feels like a heavy weight she
cannot escape from. The plaintiff shows a tendency for high emotional suffering
and depersonalization. It would be likely that if there is delay in court
proceedings, there will also be a prolonged period of stress, which can
exacerbate or increase her symptoms and decrease her well-being and her
functioning.

[
35
]

The plaintiff relies upon
Rule 9‑5(1)(b),

(c), and (d) of the
Supreme Court Civil Rules
, which permits
external facts and evidence in considering her application (such as I have just
reviewed) related to the plaintiff's treatment and her injuries. Whereas
pursuant to subrule 9-5(1)(a), no evidence is admissible. However, that latter subsection
is not relied upon by the plaintiff. Our courts have summarized what is
required under the subrules as follows.

[
36
]

In
Willow v. Chong
,
2013 BCSC 1083
at para.
20
,
Justice Fisher said that with respect to subrule 9-5(1)(b):

… a pleading is unnecessary or vexatious if
it does not go to establishing the plaintiff’s cause of action, if it does not
advance any claim known in law, where it is obvious that an action cannot
succeed, or where it would serve no useful purpose and would be a waste of the
court’s time and public resources … .

[Citations
omitted.]

[
37
]

Justice Romilly summarized the principles
applicable to both subrules (b) and (c) in the case of
Citizens for Foreign
Aid Reform Inc. v. Canadian Jewish Congress
, [1999] B.C.J. No. 2160,
1999
CanLII 5860 (S.C)
. He noted at para. 47:

An “embarrassing” and “scandalous” pleading
is one that is so irrelevant that it will involve the parties in useless
expense and will prejudice the trial of the action by involving them in a
dispute apart from the issues … .

[Citations
omitted.]

[
38
]

Justice Grauer, in
Canadian Federation of
Students v. Simon Fraser Student Society
,
2010 BCSC 1816
[
Canadian
Federation of Students
], said that with respect to subrules (c) and (d),
they involve a number of considerations as follows:

[40]      … These include whether the
pleadings are unintelligible, confusing, and difficult to understand, whether
they are so irrelevant … that they will involve the parties in useless expense
and prejudice the trial by involving them in dispute that strays far from the
issues … These considerations also encompass a pleading that is made for an
improper purpose, such as to harass and oppress the other parties, as opposed
to raising a
bona fide
defence.

[Citations
omitted.]

[
39
]

Further, with respect to subrule (d), Grauer J.
stated at para. 41:

… A pleading is an “abuse of process of the
court” not only if it attempts to re-litigate something already decided, but
also if it violates such principles as judicial economy, consistency, finality,
and the integrity of the administration of justice … .

[Citations
omitted.]

[
40
]

Applying these subrules, the plaintiff submits that the injuries
alleged in the amended notice of civil claim fall outside of the definition of ‘minor
injury’. For example, it is not an abrasion, contusion, a laceration or a
strain and that is not alleged in the amended notice of civil claim.

[
41
]

The plaintiff submits that a pain syndrome that results in serious
impairment and is not expected to improve substantially, applies to her. A psychological
or psychiatric condition is not alleged in the amended notice of civil claim. A
TMJ disorder is also not alleged in the amended notice of civil claim.

[
42
]

The plaintiff says the defendants should not be allowed to maintain
a pleading alleging injuries as minor injuries for the following reasons. The
minor injury defence is unnecessary, scandalous, frivolous or vexatious, in
light of the medical opinions. The minor injury defence will prejudice or delay
the fair trial or hearing of the proceeding because she will have to wait 15 to
17 months just for a determination by the CRT.

[
43
]

The plaintiff further submits that the minor injury defence in the
context of this case is an abuse of process because it creates a prolonged
period of stress.

[
44
]

The defendants submit that this is not a proper forum to determine
whether or not these are minor injuries. As I noted at the outset of these
reasons,
s. 133(1)
(b) provides that the determination of whether an injury
is a minor injury for motor vehicle accidents that occurred after the
CRTA

amendments, is within the exclusive jurisdiction of the CRT and is binding on
the parties, subject only to judicial review.

[
45
]

In
Delaney & Friends Cartoon Productions
Ltd. v. Radical Entertainment Inc.
,
2005 BCSC 371
, Justice Joyce stated the
following:

[21]      While evidence is admissible under
subrules (b) to (d), the court is not to engage in an assessment of the
relative merits of the parties’ cases through a detailed analysis of the
evidence. As Gray J. said in
Triathlon Ltd. v. Kirkpatrick
at paras. 31
– 32:

Evidence is
admissible with respect to an application under Rule 19(24)(b) through (d). See

Teachers Investment & Housing Cooperative Ltd. v. Jennings
,
[1991]
B.C.J. No. 3597 (B.C.S.C.), at p. 4
. However, the court should not
weigh the merits of the parties' claims. If the issues are so clear that they
could be resolved on the merits on the basis of affidavit evidence only, the
parties can pursue their remedies under Rule 18A.

The purpose of the evidence is only to
determine whether the court is satisfied that the pleading falls within a
category described in Rule 19(24)(b) through (d).

[
46
]

In my analysis, starting with Rule 9‑5(1)(b), I cannot
find that the pleading of a minor injury is either unnecessary, scandalous,
frivolous or vexatious. If the defendants are of the view that the plaintiff's
injuries fall within the definition, I am not in a position to make that
determination today, at least to the extent that it is obvious that the
pleading cannot succeed or serve no useful purpose.

[
47
]

As noted in the
Delaney
decision of Justice Joyce, the court
should not engage in an assessment of the merits of the parties' cases through
a detailed analysis of the evidence, including the medical opinions. The court
should only concern itself with whether it should be struck as a defence
because of the factors set out in subrule (1)(b).

[
48
]

Applying the principles set out by Grauer J. in the
Canadian
Federation of Students
case, I cannot find that the minor injury defence is
raised for an improper purpose, as opposed to a
bona fide
defence. Nor
can I find that it is so irrelevant that it will prejudice the trial by
involving the parties in a dispute that strays far from the issues.

[
49
]

To the contrary, as a defence its consequence is to have the issue
of the minor injury placed within the exclusive jurisdiction of the CRT. I do
not agree with the plaintiff's position that having the issue resolved at the
CRT will inevitably prejudice or delay a fair trial. In fact, it may resolve
the action without the necessity of the trial in this Court.

[
50
]

I note that in both the
Madden
and
Carter
cases, the
minor injury defence resulted in both trial dates, one a mere month away, being
adjourned. I am also not satisfied it should be struck under subrule (1)(c).

[
51
]

As for subrule (1)(d), in
Rossner v. Nystrom
,
2019 BCSC 583
at para.
43
, the court stated that
this rule “permits the court to prevent unfairness and oppressive treatment in
the context of civil actions.”

[
52
]

However, the proceedings must be so unfair as to bring the
administration of justice into disrepute. In
Rossner

at paras.
46
and 47
, the court noted the motive or status of the parties is not relevant. A
party invoking the doctrine of abuse of process bears a heavy onus and must
show that the abuse is plain and obvious.

[
53
]

I cannot come to that conclusion in this case. So, again, I am not
satisfied it should be struck under subrule (1)(d).

[
54
]

Accordingly, while I have sympathy for the plaintiff's
circumstances, I must dismiss her application.

[
55
]

I will now deal with the defendants' application.
The following is found in the response to civil claim (under the heading
Division 3 – Additional Facts):

3.         The Defendants
say and the fact is that if the Plaintiff suffered any injury in the collision
(which is not admitted but specifically denied), then any such injuries were
minor injuries as defined by the
Insurance (Vehicle) Act
and regulations thereto.

[
56
]

The pleadings go on to state (under the heading
Part 3: Legal Basis):

5.         Any injuries
suffered by the Plaintiff in the collision are minor injuries as defined by the

Insurance (Vehicle) Act
and regulations thereto, and as a result any amount
recoverable by the Plaintiff for non‑pecuniary loss are subject to the
prescribed amounts set out in that Act and the regulations made under it.

[
57
]

I have reviewed the responses to the civil claims in both
Madden

and
Carter
and note that the defendants specifically pled not only that
the plaintiff's injuries were minor injuries as defined in the
Insurance
(Vehicle) Act
but they also specifically pled that the plaintiff's claims were
within the jurisdiction of, and ought to be adjudicated by the CRT pursuant to
the
CRTA
and amendments and regulations. In
Carter
, this required
an amendment to the response to civil claim as a minor injury defence was not
initially raised.

[
58
]

The defendants before me seek an order pursuant
to
s. 16.1(2)
of the
CRTA
. This is the same section referenced in
both
Madden
and
Carter
cases as support for the stays. This subsection
requires a party to allege the jurisdiction of the CRT in addition to the
injury being a minor injury.
Section 16.1(2)
(a) states:

… if, in a court proceeding, a party alleges
that a matter in a proceeding before the court relates to a minor injury within
the jurisdiction of the tribunal under section 133(1)(b) or (c), the court must
stay the proceeding until the tribunal determines, as applicable,

(a)        in the case of
an accident claim under subsection 133(1)(b), whether an injury is a minor
injury …

[
59
]

The plaintiff refers to a text from Professor Sullivan,
Construction
of Statutes
, 7th ed. (Markham: LexisNexis, 2022), which summarizes the "presumption
against tautology." Professor Sullivan noted, “Every word and provision
found in a statute is supposed to have a meaning and a function. For this
reason, [the] courts should avoid, as much as possible, adopting
interpretations that render any portion of the statute meaningless or pointless
or redundant.”

[
60
]

In
Wormell v. Insurance Corp. of British
Columbia
,
2011 BCCA 166
, Chief Justice Finch held at para. 22:

… All words in a
provision are to be taken to have a meaning. To interpret this clause as ICBC
would, that whenever the crane is being operated it is at a site, effectively
strikes out or renders superfluous the words "at a site where the attached
equipment is being operated”.

[
61
]

Chief Justice Finch was referring to s. 72 (2) of the
regulations under the
Insurance (Motor Vehicle) Act
.

[
62
]

Lastly, Justice Elwood stated the following in
Brar
v. Feng
,
2022 BCSC 1719
, at para.
13
:

I am also alive
to the rule of statutory interpretation that a provision that limits a
plaintiff's right to bring an action is to be construed strictly, with any
ambiguity resolved in favour of the plaintiff:
Berardinelli v. Ontario
Housing Corp
,
1978 CanLII 42 (SCC)
, [1979] 1 SCR 275, at 280.

[
63
]

I agree with Elwood J’s statement of the rule of statutory
interpretation that any provisions that limits the rights of a party to pursue
injury claims in this Court must and should be strictly construed. Accordingly,
I find that the response to the civil claim fails to meet the criteria
expressly set out in
s. 16.1(2)
of the
CRTA
.

[
64
]

I further find that the authority relied upon by the defendants,
namely
Horvath v. Thring
,
2000 BCSC 123
, to be distinguishable on its
facts as it relates to a Worker's Compensation case which, by legislative
enactments, absolutely barred the action being commenced by the plaintiff. It did
not require a defence to be pled, as the making of orders finding liability
against the defendants in face of statutory bars was unlawful.

[
65
]

In the case before me, the plaintiff has a right of action in this Court
and subject to appropriate pleadings such as found in
Madden
and
Carter
,
she should be allowed to pursue that right of action. Therefore, I also dismiss
the defendants application but grant them leave to renew the application upon amendments
to their pleadings.

[
66
]

However, it is my hope that the parties will take a step back and
consider other options to resolve this matter that perhaps will lead to a
resolution sooner than later.

[
67
]

In summary, both applications are dismissed.

[
68
]

Costs?

(SUBMISSIONS ON COSTS)

[
69
]

THE COURT: Costs will be in the cause.

“Master Krentz”
